speaker: Unknown
en: The first thing I want to talk about, it's something that stood out in our jamming on what to talk about is, the way you think about designing teams.
zh: 我想谈的第一件事，是我们在讨论聊什么时脱颖而出的一点，就是你如何看待团队设计。

speaker: Unknown
en: The way you described it to me is you like to design teams like a terrorist organization.
zh: 你向我描述的方式是，你喜欢像设计一个恐怖组织那样设计团队。

speaker: Unknown
en: Yeah, yeah.
zh: 是啊，是啊。

speaker: Unknown
en: I should probably workshop this one a little bit.
zh: 这个说法我大概应该先打磨一下。

speaker: Unknown
en: This is probably an example of the one that's better for behind closed doors.
zh: 这大概是一个更适合关起门来说的例子。

speaker: Unknown
en: But yeah, I actually talked to the Chief People Officer at Discord about this, and I think she was simultaneously horrified and intrigued in a way, which credit to her for not judging me right off the bat.
zh: 不过是的，我其实和 Discord 的首席人事官聊过这个，我觉得她在某种程度上既震惊又好奇， credit 到她，她没有立马对我下判断。

speaker: Unknown
en: But yeah, I think it comes from essentially two primary beliefs from me.
zh: 不过是的，我认为这基本上源于我的两个主要信念。

speaker: Unknown
en: One is that there's actually a hidden cost to collaborating that no one really internalizes extremely well, meaning you'll never hear really any executive at any company be like, "Stop collaborating."
zh: 第一个是，协作其实有一种隐藏成本，没有人真正很好地内化它，也就是说，你永远不会听到任何公司的任何高管说“停止协作”。

speaker: Unknown
en: And to me, that's like a warning sign.
zh: 而对我来说，这是一个警告信号。

speaker: Unknown
en: Collaboration comes with incredible coordination costs, and coordination costs essentially assure that you're moving as slow as the slowest node in the system.
zh: 协作伴随着巨大的协调成本，而协调成本基本上保证了你的移动速度和系统中速度最慢的节点一样慢。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so, I try and aggressively internalize the cost of collaboration sometimes.
zh: 所以，我有时会非常激进地去内化协作的成本。

speaker: Unknown
en: And then I think the second thing separately from this is that at high growth companies especially, and so many of the people that listen to your podcast I think aspire to be at these types of companies, product managers should be in a position where they're making decisions that the founders would've made sometimes six months ago.
zh: 然后我认为第二件事，与此分开来看，是在高增长公司里尤其是如此，而我想你的播客的这么多听众都渴望身处这类公司，产品经理应该处于这样的位置：他们做出的决定是创始人有时六个月前才会做的决定。

speaker: Unknown
en: Definitely like a year or two ago, these are decisions that the founders themselves would've made.
zh: 肯定像一两年前的样子，这些是创始人自己会做的决定。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so, set aside violence for a moment.
zh: 所以，先把暴力放一边。

speaker: Unknown
en: I'm not saying that I design my teams for violence, but a good terrorist organization essentially has two things.
zh: 我不是说我设计团队是为了暴力，但一个好的恐怖组织本质上拥有两样东西。

speaker: Unknown
en: One is, it has this ideological culture that everyone understands why they are doing what they're doing.
zh: 其一是，它有一种意识形态文化，每个人都明白自己为什么做自己正在做的事。

speaker: Unknown
en: And then it has a very, very clear organizational structure of who can be trusted with which decision.
zh: 然后它有一个非常非常清晰的组织结构，明确谁可以被信任做出哪种决定。

speaker: Unknown
en: And I think creating a culture where there's a very clear ideological, almost religious level goal, essentially that the strategy is almost like a religion to the entire team.
zh: 而我认为，创造一种文化，其中有一个非常清晰的意识形态层面的、几乎是宗教级的目标，本质上让战略对整个团队来说几乎像一种宗教。

speaker: Unknown
en: And an organizational structure where people understand who are the directly responsible individuals, who's single-threaded on something, who's the throat to choke, use whatever MBA, blah, blah, blah-ism you want.
zh: 以及一种组织结构，让人们明白谁是可以直接负责的个人，谁在某个事情上是单线程的，谁是那个可以掐住的喉咙，随你用哪个 MBA 之类的什么主义。

speaker: Unknown
en: I think the combination of those two things can be leveraged in a way such that you don't need to over-collaborate, and you can be assured of achieving the results that you wanted as if you had collaborated.
zh: 我认为这两者的结合可以这样利用：你不需要过度协作，却可以确保取得你想要的结果，就好像你协作过一样。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so, I think the components of what is this great ideological setup, a lot of things I focus on, for example, because I think oftentimes the head of product at high growth companies where the founders are still in charge, the head of product is really like a vessel for their vision.
zh: 所以，我认为关于这个伟大的意识形态设置包含哪些要素，我关注的很多事情是，例如，因为我认为在高增长公司里，当创始人仍然掌权时，产品负责人实际上是他们愿景的容器。

speaker: Unknown
en: And both with Snap and at Discord where I had the privilege of working with the founders in both cases, I tried to take and absorb and internalize their vision and then create small phrases and language that could be used and repeated that were essentially shortcuts or almost like synecdoches of the whole strategy.
zh: 无论是在 Snap 还是在 Discord，这两种情况我都有幸与创始人共事，我都尝试去获取、吸收和内化他们的愿景，然后创造一些可以拿来使用和重复的小短语和语言，它们本质上是整个战略的快捷方式，或者几乎像是整个战略的提喻。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so yeah, I could go more into that, but that's how I think of it.
zh: 所以是啊，我可以再深入讲讲，但这就是我的想法。

speaker: Unknown
en: And obviously, giving it branding that I'm designing it like a terrorist organization at least gets people's attention, but maybe I need to workshop that a little bit.
zh: 而且显然，给它加上“我像设计恐怖组织那样设计团队”这个品牌，至少能引起人们的注意，但也许我需要打磨一下这个说法。

speaker: Unknown
en: No, you don't, this is perfect.
zh: 不，你不用，这就很完美。

speaker: Unknown
en: This is exactly what I was hoping this conversation would be.
zh: 这正是我希望这场对话成为的样子。

speaker: Unknown
en: So just to be very clear about the elements of the terrorist organization that we want to keep, one is this idea of autonomy, essentially trusting people further down in case the leaders get caught or are incommunicative.
zh: 所以为了非常清楚地说明我们想保留的恐怖组织的要素，其一是自主性这个理念，本质上是更进一步地信任更下层的人，以防领导者被抓或失去联络。

speaker: Unknown
en: So basically, giving more autonomy to folks further down the chain.
zh: 所以基本上，就是给链条更下游的人更多自主权。

speaker: Unknown
en: And then two is having a very clear mission, ideology, you might say, so that everyone's very aligned and decisions are quick and that kind of thing.
zh: 然后第二是有非常清晰的使命，可以说是意识形态，这样每个人都非常对齐，决策很快，诸如此类。

speaker: Unknown
en: Yeah, yeah.
zh: 是啊，是啊。

en: That, [inaudible 00:10:10]-

speaker: Unknown
en: It's interesting because I've heard many people describe, you want to build a cult, and this is not that different because cults are very effective at getting stuff done-
zh: 这很有意思，因为我听过很多人说，你要建立一个邪教，这并没有太大不同，因为邪教非常擅长把事情做成——

speaker: Peter Sellis
en: It is-
zh: 它是——

speaker: SPEAKER_0
en: ... for people.
zh: ……对人们来说。

speaker: Unknown
en: It is not.
zh: 它不是。

speaker: Unknown
en: Yeah.
zh: 是啊。

speaker: Unknown
en: You can't spell culture without cult.
zh: 你没法拼出 culture 这个词而不包含 cult。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so I think, yeah, it is not very different from that.
zh: 所以我觉得，是的，这和那个没有太大不同。

speaker: Unknown
en: I think there are elements of a cult that are more about the person leading the cult, whereas terrorist organizations are more about a higher power or a religion or ideology.
zh: 我认为邪教有更多是关于领导邪教的那个人，而恐怖组织更多是关于一个更高的力量、一种宗教或意识形态。

speaker: Unknown
en: So that's why I tended more towards that.
zh: 所以这就是为什么我更倾向于后者。

speaker: Unknown
en: But yeah, I think you could read up on a couple of cults and then just take it all the way to the penultimate moment before they do the thing that makes them well known as a cult and you probably could learn a lot, honestly.
zh: 不过是的，我觉得你可以研究几个邪教，然后只学到倒数第二步为止——也就是在它们做那件让它们广为人知为邪教的事情之前——说实话你大概能学到很多。

speaker: Unknown
en: There's a lot of alpha in that.
zh: 这里面有很多 alpha。

speaker: Unknown
en: Speaking of a higher power, a fun fact about you is you managed Nikita Bier, who came on the podcast, one of the most popular episodes of the podcast, quite a character, was head of product for X recently for I think a year.
zh: 说到更高的力量，关于你的一个趣事是你管理过 Nikita Bier，他上过这个播客，是播客最受欢迎的几期之一，非常有个性的一个人，最近在 X 担任产品负责人，我想大概有一年。

speaker: Unknown
en: Very few people have worked with Nikita, I'm curious what it was like to actually manage Nikita, work with Nikita.
zh: 很少有人和 Nikita 共事过，我很好奇实际管理 Nikita、和 Nikita 共事是什么感觉。

speaker: Unknown
en: Yeah, Nikita was on my team at Discord.
zh: 是的，Nikita 当时在我 Discord 的团队里。

speaker: Unknown
en: We acquired his startup and he was on the team at Discord for almost, or over a year, with some phenomenal engineers that came along with him.
zh: 我们收购了他的创业公司，他在 Discord 团队待了差不多，或者说超过一年，还带来了一些非常出色的工程师。

speaker: Unknown
en: I think managing Nikita, that's a very loose term of use of the word manage.
zh: 我觉得管理 Nikita，用“管理”这个词是非常宽松的说法。

speaker: Unknown
en: I think much like, yeah, you don't manage Nikita, you only seek to control him or direct him.
zh: 我觉得就像，是的，你没法管理 Nikita，你只能寻求控制他或者引导他。

speaker: Unknown
en: I liken it a lot to... Nikita's an awesome personality and just actual operator in the product space, pretty much one of one, and I have a ton of respect for a lot of the stuff that he does.
zh: 我经常把它比作……Nikita 是一个很棒的个性人物，也是产品领域真正的实干家，几乎是独一无二的，我对他做的很多事情都非常尊重。

speaker: Unknown
en: I think of him a lot like Liam Neeson in the Taken movie series.
zh: 我常把他比作《飓风营救》电影系列里的 Liam Neeson。

speaker: Unknown
en: Yeah, if your daughter gets kidnapped, he has a very special set of skills and he's going to employ those skills, and those skills are very hard to come by and very useful in certain situations.
zh: 是的，如果你女儿被绑架了，他有一套非常特别的技能，他会运用这些技能，这些技能非常难得，而且在某些情况下非常有用。

speaker: Unknown
en: But then when you need him to raise the daughter or buy some groceries or stuff like that, all he knows how to do is just kill everybody in the grocery store or something like that.
zh: 但当你需要他去抚养女儿或者买点杂货之类的事情时，他唯一会做的就是去把杂货店里所有人都杀掉之类的。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so no, he's yeah, an incredible person to work with when you have him on the areas that he's an expert in and truly one of one, from that perspective.
zh: 所以，不，当你让他做他擅长的专业领域时，他是一个非常了不起的共事者，从那个角度来说真正是独一无二的。

speaker: Unknown
en: How do you feel about having folks like that on your team?
zh: 你对团队里有这样的人有什么感受？

speaker: Unknown
en: I mean, a lot of people talk about having very distinct, I don't know, different people for different roles, and sometimes you need someone like that just, who drives home.
zh: 我是说，很多人都在谈论拥有非常独特的、不同的人担任不同的角色，有时候你就是需要这样一个人，就是能一锤定音的人。

speaker: Unknown
en: I think it's essential to be able to create an organization that can adopt that type of talent.
zh: 我觉得能够打造一个能吸纳这种类型人才的组织是至关重要的。

speaker: Unknown
en: I view it as a failure state if you have product orgs that can't essentially handle really spiky talent.
zh: 如果你有一个产品组织却本质上无法应对非常尖刺型人才，我认为那是一种失败状态。

speaker: Unknown
en: I mean, Nikita took it to extremes.
zh: 我是说，Nikita 把这一点推向了极致。

speaker: Unknown
en: You remember when he was on Intro doing that thing?
zh: 你还记得他上 Intro 做那个事情的时候吗？

speaker: Unknown
en: At one point I was trying to get a one-on-one with him who, by the way, he reported up into me, and I couldn't get him.
zh: 有一次我想和他开一对一，顺便说一句，他是向我汇报的，但我联系不上他。

speaker: Unknown
en: So I was like, "Dude, if you don't fucking answer my DMs, I'm going to go on Intro and book you so I can just have a one-on-one with you right now."
zh: 所以我就说：“老兄，如果你再他妈不回我的私信，我就去 Intro 上预约你，这样我就能现在马上和你开一对一了。”

speaker: Unknown
en: Luckily, we didn't get to that, he answered.
zh: 幸好我们没走到那一步，他回复了。

speaker: Unknown
en: I think I hit him up on four different messaging apps before I got hold of him.
zh: 我觉得在我联系上他之前，我在四个不同的通讯应用上给他发了消息。

speaker: Unknown
en: But yeah, I think this ability to handle spikiness, to build teams that can essentially adopt the type of talent that isn't necessarily the perfect 9:00 to 5:00 employee from a product perspective is...
zh: 不过是的，我认为这种应对尖刺性的能力，打造能够吸纳那种从产品角度看并不一定是完美的朝九晚五员工的人才的团队是……

speaker: Unknown
en: I look up a lot from a management style to Phil Jackson, the coach of the Bulls.
zh: 在管理风格上，我从 Phil Jackson 身上学到很多，公牛队的教练。

speaker: Unknown
en: And Lakers.
zh: 还有湖人队。

speaker: Unknown
en: And the Lakers.
zh: 还有湖人队。

speaker: Unknown
en: I think his ability to mesh talent of very different types that literally does not get along otherwise to create these winning teams, to have done it both as a player and as a coach in two different places, to use philosophies from Eastern philosophies, Western philosophies to combine all this stuff.
zh: 我觉得他有能力把那些平常根本合不来的、类型非常不同的人才融合起来，打造出这些夺冠球队，而且无论是作为球员还是教练，在两个不同的地方都做到了，运用东方哲学、西方哲学来把这一切结合起来。

speaker: Unknown
en: I think he's one of the most meaningful leaders from a leadership styles perspective, of the last half century.
zh: 我认为从领导风格的角度来说，他是过去半个世纪最有分量的领导者之一。

speaker: Unknown
en: And I think the thing about product, especially when it comes to consumer and anything that involves more creativity and taste, is I think of a lot of product leaders more like bands putting out albums.
zh: 而且我觉得产品的特点，尤其是涉及消费级和任何需要更多创造力与品味的东西，是我把很多产品领导者看作发专辑的乐队。

speaker: Unknown
en: And you can love a band, but sometimes they have a dud album.
zh: 你可以喜欢一个乐队，但有时候他们会出一张烂专辑。

speaker: Unknown
en: And what you do with the band as a fan during that time, do you stay a fan?
zh: 而作为粉丝，在那段时间你会怎么对待这个乐队？你还继续当粉丝吗？

speaker: Unknown
en: Do you still listen to the album?
zh: 你还会听那张专辑吗？

speaker: Unknown
en: Do you ride it through?
zh: 你会坚持挺过去吗？

speaker: Unknown
en: Do you just listen to the old stuff?
zh: 还是只听他们的老歌？

speaker: Unknown
en: That's kind of how I think of a lot of the spikier product managers that I've worked with, which is just like, man, sometimes they whiff on an album, but if I still believe in them as an artist, I'll stick with them.
zh: 我对我共事过的很多比较难搞的产品经理就是这种看法，就是，天呐，有时候他们搞砸一张专辑，但如果我仍然相信他们作为艺术家的能力，我就会继续支持他们。

speaker: Unknown
en: Something that, coming back to Nikita but going in a different direction, when he came on the podcast, this line that he's like, "I'm honored to be on a podcast about product management, as someone that doesn't believe product management is real."
zh: 有一件事，说回 Nikita 但换个方向，他来这个播客的时候，说过一句话，他说：“作为一个不相信产品管理是真实存在的人，我很荣幸能上一个关于产品管理的播客。”

speaker: Unknown
en: And it's funny that he went on to be Head of Product at X, but this connects to something that I know you believe, which is that most product managers are bad and are often net negative to the company.
zh: 有意思的是，他后来成了 X 的产品负责人，但这联系到我知道你相信的一件事，那就是大多数产品经理都很差，而且对公司来说往往是净负面的。

speaker: Unknown
en: Talk about that, and just why you think the median PM is not actually good.
zh: 聊聊这个吧，为什么你认为中位数的产品经理其实并不好。

speaker: Unknown
en: I feel like this might have been a contrarian take during the ZIRP era, but now I think it's bleeding into the mainstream of holding a higher bar for a product management.
zh: 我感觉在 ZIRP 时代这可能是一个反主流的观点，但现在我觉得它正在渗入主流，也就是对产品管理持有更高的标准。

speaker: Unknown
en: And it is funny, you have this kind of... Because you had Tom, the CPO of Whatnot-
zh: 而且很有意思，你有这种……因为你也请过 Tom,Whatnot 的 CPO——

speaker: Unknown
en: Whatnot, mm-hmm.
zh: Whatnot,嗯哼。

speaker: Peter Sellis
en: ... as well, to say something similar, and I think I agreed with a lot of the stuff he said. And I think by the way, I think some of his most senior PMs are actually former Snap PMs from my team at Snap.
zh: ……也说过类似的话，我觉得他说的大部分内容我都同意。顺便说一句，我觉得他手下一些最资深的产品经理其实是我 Snap 团队出来的前 Snap 产品经理。

speaker: Unknown
en: Oh, wow.
zh: 哦，哇。

speaker: Unknown
en: Which is great because it, I think, verifies a lot of this.
zh: 这很棒，因为我觉得这印证了很多这种说法。

speaker: Unknown
en: But yeah, now a bunch of self-hating PMs who've made a bunch of money being PMs are now like, "Oh, PMs are bad."
zh: 但是 yeah,现在有一堆自我厌恶的产品经理，靠当产品经理赚了一大笔钱，现在却说：“哦,PM 都很差。”

speaker: Unknown
en: But no, I think there's actually a mathematical explanation for this.
zh: 但不,我觉得这其实有一个数学上的解释。

speaker: Unknown
en: First of all, I think any craft that is... especially when you're at the top end of any kind of skill that is normally distributed, you're at the tail end of the distribution.
zh: 首先，我觉得任何手艺……尤其是当你处于任何一种正态分布技能的顶端时，你是在分布的尾部。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so for product management, if the skill of product management is normally distributed across the population, the ones who are actually product managers are all the way on the right-hand side of the distribution.
zh: 所以对于产品管理来说，如果产品管理的技能在人群中是正态分布的，那么真正成为产品经理的人全都位于分布的右手边。

speaker: Unknown
en: So you lop that off and it becomes a power distribution.
zh: 所以你把那段切掉之后，它就变成了一个幂律分布。

speaker: Unknown
en: And for any power distribution, the median is going to be far below the average.
zh: 而对于任何幂律分布，中位数都会远低于平均值。

speaker: Unknown
en: Most people are on the left side of it.
zh: 大多数人都分布在左侧。

speaker: Unknown
en: And I think this actually gets excessively emphasized within product management for two reasons.
zh: 而我觉得这一点在产品管理内部被过度放大了，有两个原因。

speaker: Unknown
en: One, especially during the ZIRP era, it became essentially the most lucrative career in tech for non-technical people.
zh: 第一，尤其是在 ZIRP 时代，它基本上成了科技行业里非技术人最赚钱的职业。

speaker: Unknown
en: So, it has a very subjective definition, which is part of the reason why your podcast has been so valuable to people over the years because they're like, "What do I need to do to be one?"
zh: 所以，它有一个非常主观的定义，这也是为什么你的播客多年来对人们如此有价值的原因之一，因为他们会想：“我要做什么才能成为一个 PM?”

speaker: Unknown
en: And so once you're in it, you're being compensated essentially as if you're on a technical ladder, so you have a very high incentive to remain part of it.
zh: 所以一旦你入了这一行，你的薪酬基本上是按技术职级来给的，所以你有非常强的动机要留在这行里。

speaker: Unknown
en: If you're very good at it, the skills you develop as a product leader are almost perfect for either other executive roles, just like overall leadership roles, or starting your own company.
zh: 如果你非常擅长这件事，你作为产品领导者发展出的技能几乎完美适用于其他高管角色，比如整体领导力角色，或者创办自己的公司。

speaker: Unknown
en: So you're on the right-hand side of the distribution, the great product managers are exiting the system.
zh: 所以你处于分布的右手边，优秀的产品经理正在退出这个体系。

speaker: Unknown
en: They're becoming founders, they're becoming executives, etc.
zh: 他们成了创始人、成了高管，等等。

speaker: Unknown
en: And on the other side of the distribution, anybody who's in is doing anything possible to stay in.
zh: 而在分布的另一侧，任何还在里面的人都在想尽一切办法留在里面。

speaker: Unknown
en: So the distribution, it just becomes more weighted, weighted, weighted, like this.
zh: 所以这个分布就变得越来越偏向，越来越偏向，越来越偏向，像这样。

speaker: Unknown
en: And I think during ZIRP, you saw this and there were memes about it and stuff like that, and maybe there's been some correction.
zh: 我觉得在 ZIRP 期间你看到了这个现象，有各种梗图之类的东西，也许后来有过一些纠正。

speaker: Unknown
en: But yeah, I think mathematically, it's set up to be this profession where the median product manager is actually probably pretty bad.
zh: 但是 yeah,我觉得从数学上讲,这个职业天然就是这样设定的：中位数的产品经理其实很可能相当差。

speaker: Unknown
en: Do you feel like it's getting better?
zh: 你觉得情况在变好吗？

speaker: Unknown
en: And do you think...
zh: 而且你觉得……

speaker: Unknown
en: There's something I think about a lot that a lot of people say that, "PMs suck, they're useless," and I find that that's usually the case because they've just not worked with a great PM, and a lot of people haven't worked with great PMs.
zh: 有一个我经常想的事情，很多人说“PM 都很烂、没用”，我发现情况通常是这样是因为他们只是没和一个优秀的 PM 共事过，而很多人都沒有和优秀的 PM 共事过。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so it makes the whole profession look bad and sound bad when a lot of people have, as you described, are working with these kind of mediocre PMs.
zh: 所以这就让整个职业看起来很差、听起来很差，因为正如你所说，很多人一起工作的是那种平庸的 PM。

speaker: Unknown
en: Thoughts there?
zh: 对此你怎么看？

speaker: Unknown
en: Yeah, I think you're exactly right.
zh: Yeah,我觉得你说得完全对。

speaker: Unknown
en: I've also noticed this.
zh: 我也注意到了这一点。

speaker: Unknown
en: I feel like so much in the world right now is explained by some form of the midwit meme in some way or another.
zh: 我感觉现在世界上很多事情都可以用某种形式的 midwit 梗来解释。

speaker: Unknown
en: But yeah, I think you're exactly right.
zh: 但是 yeah,我觉得你说得完全对。

speaker: Unknown
en: That is a second order effect of this kind of distribution that I think governs the whole profession.
zh: 那是这种我认为支配着整个职业的分布的二阶效应。

speaker: Unknown
en: I do think it's getting better, because I think, again, a lot of people reference the ZIRP era, but I truly feel like when interest rates go down, that means opportunity costs are lower.
zh: 我确实认为情况在变好，因为我觉得，again,很多人都在引用 ZIRP 时代，但我真心觉得当利率下降时，意味着机会成本更低。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so when opportunity costs are lower, people are doing things like just hiring that extra person, doing stuff like that.
zh: 所以当机会成本更低时，人们就会去做那种多招一个人的事情，诸如此类。

speaker: Unknown
en: But these opportunity costs I think are higher than are internalized because of some of the stuff we started talking about, that a lot of these costs are not internalized.
zh: 但我觉得这些机会成本比被内化认知的更高，因为我们一开始聊到的一些内容，很多这类成本并没有被内化。

speaker: Unknown
en: And we can talk about this, but I've been really focused on developing a system for evaluating product managers, not just the person, but the person and the place that they are at that time, to make sure that the team is actually just net positive.
zh: 我们可以聊这个，但我一直非常专注于开发一套评估产品经理的体系，不只是评估这个人，而是评估这个人以及他们当时所处的环境，以确保这个团队是真正的净正向。

speaker: Unknown
en: And in my experience, and we can talk about what some of those methods are, but in my experience, the way this ends up is that I really don't hear great engineers complain about product managers that much, because great engineers, A, they know how to bend product managers to their will.
zh: 根据我的经验——我们可以聊聊其中一些方法是什么——根据我的经验，最终的结果是，我基本上很少听到优秀的工程师抱怨产品经理，因为优秀的工程师，第一，他们知道怎么让产品经理屈从于自己的意志。

speaker: Unknown
en: They get the use out of them that they want.
zh: 他们能从产品经理那里得到自己想要的东西。

speaker: Unknown
en: And B, they just don't put up with bad ones, so they don't get assigned or they don't get to work with bad product managers.
zh: 第二，他们根本不会忍受差的 PM,所以他们不会被分配、也不会和差的产品经理一起工作。

speaker: Unknown
en: I think ironically in a midwit meme or the horseshoe theory of things, really bad engineers also don't complain about product managers because they know they can just hide behind their decisions and stuff like that.
zh: 我觉得讽刺的是，按照中智梗图或者事物蹄铁理论的逻辑，真正差的工程师也不会抱怨产品经理，因为他们知道自己可以躲在产品经理的决策后面之类的东西。

speaker: Unknown
en: So, it's really just the ones in the middle that are complaining.
zh: 所以，真正在抱怨的其实只有中间那批人。

speaker: Unknown
en: I do want to ask about Snap.
zh: 我想问问 Snap 的事。

speaker: Unknown
en: I feel like it's a company that doesn't feel like it lived up to the potential of what I think Evan and everyone imagined it could be.
zh: 我感觉它是一家没有实现我认为 Evan 和所有人想象中那种潜力的公司。

speaker: Unknown
en: I imagine the main reason from, and I had Evan on the podcast, is just the users that it's going after are just hard to monetize.
zh: 我猜主要原因，我请过 Evan 上播客，就是它瞄准的用户群太难变现了。

speaker: Unknown
en: Is that the core of what has kept Snap from becoming a bigger success, or is there more to it?
zh: 这是阻止 Snap 取得更大成功的核心原因吗，还是说背后还有更多原因？

speaker: Unknown
en: I'll try and be as objective as possible, Lenny, because this is a little bit of my life's work and maybe I do have some level of chip on my shoulder, or... Yeah, I'll try and be as objective as possible.
zh: Lenny，我会尽量保持客观，因为这多少算是我毕生的事业，也许我确实心里有点不服气，或者……对，我会尽量保持客观。

speaker: Unknown
en: So I'll say two things, maybe three things about Snap from a monetization perspective, at least an ads monetization perspective.
zh: 关于 Snap，从变现的角度，至少从广告变现的角度，我来说两件事，也许三件事。

speaker: Unknown
en: And then we could talk about they've had a lot of success with Snapchat plus and subscription products in general are doing well, but ads are truly the magical product market fit of consumer monetization on the internet, and there's a lot of mathematical reasons why that's true.
zh: 然后我们可以谈谈他们在 Snapchat plus 上取得了很大成功，订阅产品总体表现不错，但广告才是互联网上消费者变现真正神奇的产品市场契合点，而这一点成立有很多数学上的原因。

en: Thoughts on that opportunity?

en: Do you think that's actually a massive business opportunity for these companies, or do you think they're not understanding the actual business there?

speaker: Unknown
en: I subscribe to the Eric Seufert side of the world, of ads are the product market fit for the internet.
zh: 我认同 Eric Seufert 那一派的观点,即广告是互联网的产品市场契合点。

speaker: Unknown
en: And I still think that from a monetization standpoint, there's a number of reasons, again, mathematical, for why that is true and why I think subscription products and things like that are overrated versus ads from a consumer side of things.
zh: 我仍然认为,从变现的角度来看,有很多原因——再次强调,是数学上的原因——说明为什么这是对的,以及为什么我认为从消费者角度来看,订阅产品之类的东西被高估了,而广告被低估了。

speaker: Unknown
en: When I look at what OpenAI is doing from an advertising perspective, they are speed running all of the ads infra that is exactly what you would want and do.
zh: 当我从广告的角度看 OpenAI 在做什么时,他们正在速通所有你想要并且会去做的广告基础设施。

speaker: Unknown
en: At Discord, I call this last mover advantage because we've learned so much and we're at a certain place with online advertising... And really Meta and the team there from 2010 through 2020 really deserves, I think, most of the credit for this.
zh: 在 Discord,我把这称为后发者优势,因为我们学到了很多,而在线广告已经发展到了某个阶段……实际上,Meta 和他们 2010 年到 2020 年间的团队,我认为最值得为此居功。

speaker: Unknown
en: What drives a modern ads marketplace and auction is essentially a solved problem, and OpenAI is speed running all of the components of that.
zh: 驱动一个现代广告市场和拍卖的东西,本质上是一个已经被解决的问题,而 OpenAI 正在速通其中的所有组件。

speaker: Unknown
en: And I do think that the mechanism, the mathematical mechanism, which is essentially a modified VCG, I think Vickrey-Clarke-Groves auction mechanism, this mathematical mechanism is the correct way to build an ads auction in even a chat environment, in ChatGPT.
zh: 而且我确实认为,那个机制——那个数学机制,本质上是一个改进版的 VCG,即 Vickrey-Clarke-Groves 拍卖机制——这个数学机制是在即使是聊天环境中、在 ChatGPT 中构建广告拍卖的正确方式。

speaker: Unknown
en: And what I mean by that is I think where the innovation came from Meta was not just that the highest bidder, and I'm oversimplifying like crazy, but not just that the highest bidder wins, but that the organic value of an advertisement and an advertiser to that user should be factored into their bid, such that you essentially have to pay more as an advertiser to reach people who may not want to be reached, or may be harder to reach, or may not necessarily be as relevant to you, and this also is great because it allows you to mox both content, organic content and advertising content, on a unified auction with dollars as essentially the ultimate denominator.
zh: 我这么说的意思是,我认为 Meta 的创新之处不仅在于出价最高者获胜——我在极度简化——而在于一条广告以及一个广告主对某个用户的自然价值应当被计入其出价,这样你作为广告主,要想触达那些可能不希望被触达的人,或者更难触达的人,或者对你来说相关性不一定那么高的人,本质上就必须付出更多;而且这也很好,因为它让你能够在统一拍卖中混合自然内容和广告内容,以金钱作为本质上的最终分母。

speaker: Unknown
en: And the reason that I say that this is good for chat is not necessarily that organic value is what's important here, like how much you like an ad or not in a content feed, but in chat, it probably feels like this could be replaced or augmented with essentially trust.
zh: 而我说这对聊天有利的原因,并不一定是自然价值在这里很重要——比如在内容信息流中你有多喜欢一条广告——而是在聊天中,这感觉上可能可以被本质上等同于「信任」的东西所替代或增强。

speaker: Unknown
en: If you boil this down to something very simple, it's just like, "Hey, what X should I buy?
zh: 如果把这归结为非常简单的东西,那就是:「嘿,我该买什么 X?

en: And in that moment, we have to decide should I give you the objective answer?

speaker: Unknown

zh: 你能看到我们在这方面多少有些失败……我真的不想点名批评任何人,因为我知道构建这类东西有多难。

en: It is getting a little crazy when you search for something and you have 16 ads before you get to the first thing, and you're like, "Oh shoot, is that subtly influencing my trust in the system?"

speaker: Unknown
en: And so, that's why I actually think OpenAI is speed running all the right stuff, and where the push is going to come to shove is how they instantiate it mathematically in their auction mechanism to maximize trust over the long term, because trust maximization will probably be correlated with user retention, if not causal, and with advertiser value.

speaker: Unknown
en: As we made Discord better, as we focused on performance, we were actually able to drive some of the fastest, I think if not the fastest growth, and I'm not sharing anything that's not public, since the pandemic, obviously Discord exploded during the pandemic, and this was by focusing on the thing that everybody already said we had 100% penetration of, which was intentional multiplayer gamers.
zh: 随着我们把 Discord 做得更好,随着我们聚焦性能,我们实际上实现了——我想如果不是最快的增长的话——也是最快的增长之一,我没有分享任何未公开的信息,显然 Discord 在疫情期间爆炸式增长,而这是通过聚焦那个每个人都说我们已经 100% 渗透的东西实现的,也就是有意的多人游戏玩家。

speaker: Unknown
en: Now, from there, you have a lot of options.
zh: 现在,从那里出发,你有很多选择。

speaker: Unknown
en: There are a lot of things that look like multiplayer gaming.
zh: 有很多看起来像多人游戏的东西。

speaker: Unknown
en: Crypto looks like multiplayer gaming, intense coordination costs, time sensitive, et cetera.
zh: 加密货币看起来像多人游戏,高协调成本、时间敏感,等等。

speaker: Unknown
en: Honestly, software development looks like multiplayer gaming.
zh: 说实话,软件开发看起来像多人游戏。

speaker: Unknown
en: There are a lot of things that you could build off of that core.
zh: 有很多东西你可以从这个核心之上构建出来。

speaker: Unknown
en: But by focusing on people who play games with their friends, we were actually able to identify a lot of things that brought somebody from using Discord, let's say, 10 days out of the 30 to 11 to 12 to 13.
zh: 但通过聚焦那些和他们的朋友一起玩游戏的人,我们实际上能够识别出很多能把某人的使用——比如说——从 30 天里的 10 天提升到 11 天、12 天、13 天的事情。

speaker: Unknown
en: That's actually monster growth when you think about those pockets and moving up people's L-ness, like last seven out of seven days.
zh: 当你想到这些小的增长点和把人们的 L-ness 往上移的时候——比如七天里七天最后——这实际上是惊人的增长。

speaker: Unknown
en: I think I stole that from Meta, who once again wrote a great playbook on growth.
zh: 我想我这是从 Meta 那里偷来的,他们又一次写了一本很棒的增长手册。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so focusing on that L-ness of the core consumer base, I think it just ended up being so positive in both the Snap and Discord examples.
zh: 所以聚焦核心消费者群体的这种 L-ness,我认为在 Snap 和 Discord 的例子里最终都极其正面。

speaker: Unknown
en: This is a really important lesson for people trying to grow a product.
zh: 对于想要增长一个产品的人来说,这是一个非常重要的教训。

speaker: Unknown
en: The TL;DR to me is there's always money in the banana stand.
zh: 对我来说,一句话总结就是:香蕉摊里永远有钱。

speaker: Unknown
en: We were talking earlier about building a terrorist organization.
zh: 我们之前谈到过建立一个恐怖组织。

speaker: Unknown
en: That's a great example of a phrase that if you could ascribe, in a strategy document, you could ascribe value like there's always money in the banana stand, return to your core users, make sure it's perfect for them, like there was always money in the banana stand.
zh: 这是一个很好的短语例子,如果你能在一份战略文档中赋予它价值,就像「香蕉摊里永远有钱」一样——回到你的核心用户,确保对他们来说它是完美的,就像香蕉摊里永远有钱一样。

speaker: Unknown
en: I think at Discord, it had exceptionally positive externalities because the most vocal, critical, honestly like intelligent or high-IQ user base in the world are gamers, honestly.
zh: 我认为在 Discord,它有极其正面的外部性,因为世界上最直言不讳、最挑剔、说实话最聪明或高 IQ 的用户群体就是游戏玩家,说实话。

speaker: Unknown
en: You think you've built for people who are critical about your product, who are detail oriented, unless you've built for gamers, you haven't.
zh: 你以为自己已经为那些对你的产品挑剔、注重细节的人构建了产品,除非你为游戏玩家构建过,否则你没有。

speaker: Unknown
en: And to be able to turn around and say we are focused, like here's a bug thread on Reddit, show us what's messing up.
zh: 而能够转过身来说我们是聚焦的,比如这是 Reddit 上的一个 bug 帖子,告诉我们是什么搞坏了。

speaker: Unknown
en: We don't care how small it is, how big it is, we will fix it.
zh: 我们不在乎它有多小、有多大,我们会修好它。

speaker: Unknown
en: It had this unbelievable positive externality of we are delivering for this community.
zh: 它带来了这种难以置信的正面外部性:我们在为这个社区交付。

speaker: Unknown
en: And I honestly think this is why Discord is so great and so without pure in this specific niche is because it's so laser focused on if you play games with your friends and you care about it, this product is going to, like there are people who sit in that office who will make it perfect for you forever.
zh: 而我真心认为这就是为什么 Discord 在这个特定的小众领域如此出色、如此纯粹没有杂质,因为它如此高度聚焦于:如果你和你的朋友一起玩游戏并且你在乎这件事,这个产品就会——办公室里有人会永远把它为你做到完美。

speaker: Unknown
en: So this begs the question, when does it make sense to bet on something new and try new things?
zh: 所以这就引出了一个问题,什么时候押注新东西、尝试新事物才是合理的?

speaker: Unknown
en: Because it doesn't always make sense to just continue refining and refining the one piece of product market fit that's worked.
zh: 因为并不总是只要持续打磨那一条已经被验证的产品市场契合点就够了。

speaker: Unknown
en: Any guidance to folks, and this is for consumer in particular, any guidance for when it makes sense to still make bets outside that core?
zh: 有什么建议给大家吗,尤其是针对消费级产品,什么时候在核心之外进行押注才是合理的?

speaker: Unknown
en: Yeah, I think there are two really incremental ways to think about it.
zh: 是的,我认为有两种非常渐进的思考方式。

speaker: Unknown
en: One is if you boil down the core things about your product that are really, really great that people come to it for.
zh: 第一种是,把你产品中真正、真正出色、人们因为它而来的核心要素提炼出来。

speaker: Unknown
en: So for Snap, maybe it's the camera, for Discord it's voice, and then you look to other niches, other cohorts for which that could be useful.
zh: 比如 Snap,可能是相机;Discord 是语音;然后你去寻找其他细分领域、其他人群,看这个核心对他们是否有用。

speaker: Unknown
en: It's a very like MBA-style, 2x2 type of thing.
zh: 这是一种很像 MBA 风格的、二乘二矩阵式的思路。

speaker: Unknown
en: That's I think one method to do that and you should, honestly, always be assessing that because that's an easy one.
zh: 我认为这是一种方法,而且说实话,你应该一直持续评估这一点,因为这是最容易做的。

speaker: Unknown
en: And then, I think the second thing is one of the greatest gifts is when people use your product in a way that you didn't expect or didn't ordain because they're going through extra hoops to do what they want to do with the product.
zh: 然后,我认为第二件事是,最大的礼物之一就是当人们以一种你没有预料到或没有规定的方式使用你的产品,因为他们为了用产品做自己想做的事而愿意绕额外的弯路。

speaker: Unknown
en: So whatever you're offering is so good that they're going through hoops to do that.
zh: 也就是说,你提供的东西太好了,好到他们愿意费劲去用它。

speaker: Unknown
en: For Discord, for example, a lot of it centered around communities and how people were using it to organize larger and larger communities as opposed to the 20-person gaming friend group.
zh: 以 Discord 为例,很多用法都围绕着社区,以及人们如何用它来组织越来越大的社区,而不是 20 人的游戏好友小圈子。

speaker: Unknown
en: And when people are doing that, they're essentially voting with their feet.
zh: 当人们这么做时,他们其实是在用脚投票。

speaker: Unknown
en: They're telling you, "I want to use this product for this.
zh: 他们在告诉你,“我想用这个产品来做这件事。

speaker: Unknown
en: What can you do to make it a little bit easier for me?"
zh: 你能做点什么让它对我来说更方便一点?"

speaker: Unknown
en: So it kind of is a version of that, but it's like expanding to the next thing.
zh: 所以这算是那的一种版本,但更像是扩展到下一个东西。

speaker: Unknown
en: And that's more like thinking about concentric circles.
zh: 那更像是同心圆式的思考。

speaker: Unknown
en: It's like, "Okay, we got it at the core.
zh: 就是说,“好,我们在核心上做到了。

speaker: Unknown
en: How do we expand, expand?"
zh: 我们怎么扩展、扩展?"

speaker: Unknown
en: I feel like I'm doing something with my hands here that's going to be memed, but it works.
zh: 我感觉我在这儿用手比划的动作要被做成梗图了,但确实很形象。

speaker: Unknown
en: Oh, it is.
zh: 哦,会的。

speaker: Unknown
en: We got it.
zh: 我们懂了。

speaker: Unknown
en: Okay, I'll stop.
zh: 好,我不比划了。

speaker: Unknown
en: But I think then the more Snapchat, the more innovative way to think about it is more to look at your company's philosophy around why it was built and then think about the future totally unencumbered by the present.
zh: 但我认为,更 Snapchat 式、更有创新性的思考方式是,去审视你公司的创建哲学,然后完全不受当下束缚地思考未来。

speaker: Unknown
en: No incrementality from the present, more like future casting, like back casting instead of forecasting and be like, "Okay, right now, the best way to share a moment is to pull out your phone and aim the camera at it and record."
zh: 不带任何来自当下的渐进式思维,更像是未来投射,是回溯投射(back casting)而不是预测(forecasting),然后说,“好,现在,分享一个瞬间的最好方式是掏出手机,把摄像头对准它,然后录下来。"

speaker: Unknown
en: That's very constrained by the existing technology.
zh: 这非常受现有技术的限制。

speaker: Unknown
en: If we were to envision a future of what's the future look like to be the best way, something just happened or my child just took its first steps, I'm at a concert, I just saw something really funny on the street, what's the best way to share that moment with my friends, I think that's what leads to you to something like, "Oh, probably glasses," or things like that.
zh: 如果我们去畅想未来——发生了某件事、我的孩子刚迈出第一步、我在演唱会、我刚在街上看到特别搞笑的东西——分享那个瞬间的最好方式是什么,我认为这就会引导你想到类似“哦,大概是眼镜吧”之类的东西。

speaker: Unknown
en: So this back casting method, I think, is what everybody wants to do.
zh: 所以这种回溯投射的方法,我认为,是每个人都想做的。

speaker: Unknown
en: In my experience, there are very few people that have this type of blank sheet creativity to think about the future totally unencumbered from the present.
zh: 以我的经验,很少有人具备这种白纸式的创造力,能完全摆脱当下的束缚去思考未来。

speaker: Unknown
en: Most people like to, even really creative people, remix versions of the present or I think these days most product managers go on an ayahuasca journey or travel to Japan or something and then come back and they're like, "I've solved it."
zh: 大多数人喜欢,即使是极有创造力的人,把当下进行混音再创作;或者我觉得如今大多数产品经理会去喝一次死藤水、或者去日本旅行什么的,然后回来说,“我解决了。"

speaker: Unknown
en: But very few people, I think, are very good at this version of it.
zh: 但我认为,很少有人真正擅长刚才说的那种版本。

speaker: Unknown
en: And I think a big part of this is you found product market fit, something's working, you almost take for granted how lucky you are that you found something that works.
zh: 而且我认为很重要的一点是,你找到了产品市场契合,有些东西在起作用,你几乎把“找到有效的东西是多么幸运”视为理所当然。

speaker: Unknown
en: And it may be easy to think, "Oh, we'll find the next thing now," and very few people do.
zh: 然后很容易觉得,“哦,我们现在就能找到下一个东西",但很少有人做到。

speaker: Unknown
en: Airbnb is actually a really good example of this.
zh: Airbnb 其实就是一个很好的例子。

speaker: Unknown
en: Nothing beyond the original idea has worked in a big way.
zh: 除了最初那个想法,没有什么东西在大范围内成功过。

speaker: Unknown
en: It's still basically the same core idea.
zh: 它本质上还是同一个核心想法。

speaker: Unknown
en: I've worked there for a long time and nothing has significantly impacted the growth trajectory, other than just exactly what you just described, continuing to make the core experience better, more supply, more demand.
zh: 我在那里工作了很长时间,没有任何东西显著影响过增长轨迹,除了你刚才描述的那种——持续把核心体验做得更好、更多供给、更多需求。

speaker: Unknown
en: So I think this is a really profound point for people to take in.
zh: 所以我认为这是一个非常深刻的、值得人们吸收的观点。

speaker: Unknown
en: It's also like you can keep teams leaner this way, things like that.
zh: 这也意味着你可以用这种方式保持团队更精简,诸如此类。

speaker: Unknown
en: The biggest risk is its kind of like that, I think it's a Nassim Taleb meme of "1,001 days in the life of a Thanksgiving turkey-"
zh: 最大的风险是,有点像——我想那是 Nassim Taleb 的一个梗——“感恩节火鸡生命中的 1001 天——"

speaker: Unknown
en: Turkey.
zh: 火鸡。

speaker: Unknown
en: ... where it's just like, yeah, everything's getting better and better and better until something comes along that's literally 10X better than what you're doing and it takes you to zero overnight.
zh: "……就是,一切都越来越好、越来越好、越来越好,直到某个比你正在做的事真的强 10 倍的东西出现,一夜之间把你归零。"

speaker: Unknown
en: And guarding against that, I don't have any.
zh: 而如何防范这一点,我没有任何答案。

speaker: Unknown
en: If I knew how to guard against Black Swan events like that, yeah, I think-
zh: 如果我知道如何防范那样的黑天鹅事件,嗯,我觉得——

speaker: Unknown
en: You'd be in finance.
zh: 你就去干金融了。

speaker: Unknown
en: Yeah, I'd definitely be in finance.
zh: 是啊,我绝对就去干金融了。

speaker: Unknown
en: I actually think this... We were talking a little bit, like SpaceX is probably a good example actually of a company that guards itself against this in some ways.
zh: 我其实觉得这个……我们刚才聊了一点,SpaceX 可能其实是一个很好的例子,是一家在某些方面能防范这种风险的公司。

speaker: Unknown
en: Okay.
zh: 好。

speaker: Unknown
en: Say more.
zh: 展开说说。

speaker: Unknown
en: I know your wife works at SpaceX, so you have a really unique insight into how SpaceX works and what has worked there.
zh: 我知道你妻子在 SpaceX 工作,所以你对 SpaceX 的运作方式以及那里什么有效有着非常独特的见解。

speaker: Unknown
en: Yeah, no inside information.
zh: 是的,没有内幕消息。

speaker: Unknown
en: I'm like a second party.
zh: 我算是第二方。

speaker: Unknown
en: I'm not first party, but I sleep next to a SpaceX engineer every night, so that helps.
zh: 我不是第一方,但我每天晚上都睡在一位 SpaceX 工程师旁边,所以这有帮助。

speaker: Unknown
en: Yeah, that's all you have to do.
zh: 是啊,这就是你要做的全部了。

speaker: Unknown
en: But no, I think SpaceX is the greatest American company right now, greatest company in the world, truly phenomenal on every single level.
zh: 不过说真的,我认为 SpaceX 是当今最伟大的美国公司,世界上最伟大的公司,在每一个层面上都真正非凡。

speaker: Unknown
en: And I'm talking more about SpaceX, like XAI is also doing insane stuff, but like just that.
zh: 我说的更多是 SpaceX,比如 xAI 也在做疯狂的东西,但就是说这个。

speaker: Unknown
en: And I think the best example, what I mean by guarding us a future, I don't think any company does anything close to what SpaceX does here.
zh: 我认为最好的例子,我说的「为未来守护我们」,我不认为有任何公司在这点上能接近 SpaceX 所做的。

speaker: Unknown
en: And there's a recent example, literally, I think in the last week of this perfectly, where they essentially announced some version of they are taking the Falcon 9, which is their primary launch system, the greatest launch system in the world ever by far, reusable, most cost-effective kilograms to lower earth orbit, to geostationary orbit, every country on the planet would give up their GDP to have this technology to be able to launch or reuse rides, and they're sun-setting the Falcon 9.
zh: 最近就有个例子,我想就在上周,完美地体现了这一点,他们基本上宣布了某种版本的消息:他们要让 Falcon 9 退役——那是他们的主要发射系统,有史以来遥遥领先的最伟大发射系统,可重复使用,把每公斤载荷送到近地轨道、地球同步轨道的成本效益最高,地球上每个国家都愿意拿出他们的 GDP 来换这项技术,以便能够发射或重复使用班次——而他们正在让 Falcon 9 逐步退场。

speaker: Unknown
en: And this is like Cortés-level "burn the ships upon arriving" because they're essentially saying like in order to reach our vision in the future, we need a heavier lift launch vehicle, that is Starship.
zh: 这就像科尔蒂斯级别的「抵达后烧毁船只」,因为他们基本上是在说:为了实现我们对未来的愿景,我们需要一个更大运载能力的发射载具,那就是 Starship。

speaker: Unknown
en: So starting in a few years, because they have customers and things like that, you'll no longer be able to buy rides on the Falcon 9.
zh: 所以从几年后开始,因为他们有客户之类的原因,你将不再能购买 Falcon 9 上的班次。

speaker: Unknown
en: I don't think it's for everything, but they're gradually basically telegraphing that the Falcon 9 is the past.
zh: 我不认为这适用于所有情况,但他们基本上在逐渐昭示 Falcon 9 属于过去。

speaker: Unknown
en: By the way, the Falcon 9 would be the future for literally every other country, nation state on the planet.
zh: 顺便说一句,Falcon 9 对地球上字面意义上的每一个其他国家、民族国家来说,都会是未来。

speaker: Unknown
en: It's incredible machine.
zh: 这是台令人难以置信的机器。

speaker: Unknown
en: Elon has built this culture that Clayton Christensen is dead, but he probably would shed a tear over how happy it would make him about avoiding the innovator's dilemma versus just because we have the thing that is the best, we're completely willing to build the thing that will compete against ourselves and make the thing that we built irrelevant.
zh: Elon 建立了这样一种文化,Clayton Christensen 已经去世了,但如果他能看到这里对避开创新者窘境的处理方式他大概会落泪——不是仅仅因为我们拥有最好的东西,而是我们完全愿意去建造一个与我们自己竞争的东西,让我们建造的东西变得无关紧要。

speaker: Unknown
en: I wish I had more insight into what drives that beyond maybe just Elon or that whole organization, but what I've witnessed top to bottom is everybody you talk to there is like, "Yeah, it's going to be awesome.
zh: 我希望自己能对驱动这一切的东西有更深入的了解,除了可能就是 Elon 本人或整个组织之外,但我从上到下所目睹的是,你在那里交谈的每个人都像是:「是啊,这将会很棒。

speaker: Unknown
en: Yeah, we're going to do this."
zh: 是啊,我们要做这个。」

speaker: Unknown
en: It's definitely part of the culture, maybe the cult, that they can do this even though on paper and now as a public company, it kind of looks insane.
zh: 这绝对是文化的一部分,也许是一种狂热,他们能做到这一点,尽管在纸面上,以及现在作为一家上市公司,这看起来有点疯狂。

speaker: Unknown
en: And so yeah, I think that's actually a really underrated part about SpaceX is their ability to essentially burn the ships and focus on what's next.
zh: 所以是的,我认为这其实是 SpaceX 一个非常被低估的方面:他们本质上烧毁船只并专注于下一步的能力。

speaker: Unknown
en: This to me comes well back to the original beginning of this conversation, building an org like a terrorist organization, in particular the mission.
zh: 对我来说,这正好回到了这次对话的最开头:像恐怖组织一样构建一个组织,尤其是使命。

speaker: Unknown
en: Clearly, the mission of SpaceX make humanity multi-planetary, get to Mars.
zh: 显然,SpaceX 的使命是让人类成为多行星物种,到达火星。

speaker: Unknown
en: And with that mission, I can totally see how they may be working backwards from, "In order to do this, we need this larger rocket.
zh: 有了这个使命,我完全能看出他们可能是如何从中倒推的:「为了做到这一点,我们需要这枚更大的火箭。

speaker: Unknown
en: It makes no sense to keep investing here."
zh: 继续在这里投资没有意义。」

speaker: Unknown
en: So to me, it feels very clear how they go about making these decisions.
zh: 所以对我来说,他们如何做出这些决定感觉非常清晰。

speaker: Unknown
en: Yeah, I think there's another thing about both of Elon's major, SpaceX and Tesla, I know less about Neuralink, The Boring Company, et cetera, but you look on the website, I mean now I don't know where it is, but they publish essentially 10-year plans.
zh: 是的,我认为关于 Elon 的两家主要公司,SpaceX 和 Tesla,我对 Neuralink、The Boring Company 等了解较少,还有另一件事,你看网站,我是说现在我不知道在哪了,但他们基本上发布十年计划。

speaker: Unknown
en: Nothing SpaceX is doing is not something that they didn't talk about 10 years ago.
zh: SpaceX 现在做的事情,没有一件不是他们十年前没有谈论过的。

speaker: Unknown
en: Like Tesla talked about exactly what they wanted to do with the initial Roadster, to fund the S, to fund the 3.
